Israeli defence minister rejects army chief's call to detain violent settlers, report says

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has rejected a new request from military chief of staff Eyal Zamir to authorise administrative detention orders against Israeli settlers involved in attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, Kan reported.

Zamir told Katz at a security consultation on Thursday that further steps were needed amid rising settler violence, and called for administrative detention and restraining orders against perpetrators, the report said.

Administrative detention allows suspects to be held indefinitely without charge or trial. It is widely used against Palestinians, including children, but Katz halted its use against Jewish Israelis in November 2024. He has, in fact,  repeatedly boasted of doing so, while expanding its use against Palestinians.

Dozens of restraining orders, which bar individuals from parts of the West Bank, are awaiting Shin Bet approval, according to Kan. Channel 12 reported that 70 people suspected of involvement in such attacks were arrested in recent weeks, but Israeli courts released all of them without indictments.

Shin Bet chief David Zini, who belongs to the Orthodox nationalist Hardal camp, has consistently objected to movement bans. He has been accused of undermining the agency's unit tasked with tackling settler violence.

The PGSA blacklists ships it accuses of breaking its Hormuz transit rules, threatening fines, detention or confiscation. Its list passed 120 vessels in October.

According to the weekly overview, three tankers were struck by unknown projectiles within about 17 minutes on 22 November while heading east through the Strait of Hormuz. All three continued their voyages.

UKMTO documented 10 incidents in the week to 25 November, seven of them in the Strait of Hormuz.

Combined transits remain roughly 65 percent below pre-conflict levels, with 166 outbound and 173 inbound crossings last week. About 70 percent were energy carriers, and more vessels are using the southern route.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] South Africa accused of hypocrisy over Israeli offshore oil project
item.description:
South Africa accused of hypocrisy over Israeli offshore oil project

Submitted by Azad Essa on Wed, 11/25/2026 - 20:09
South African activists say the government's approval of an Israeli company's offshore oil deal contradicts its climate commitments and legal action against Israel at the ICJ
South Africans rally in Sea Point, Cape Town, on 3 October 2026, ahead of the third anniversary of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza (Esa Alexander/Reuters)
Off

South African activists have accused the government of hypocrisy over its decision to approve an Israeli company's takeover of an offshore oil and gas project, saying the move undermines Pretoria's climate commitments and its case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

More than two months after Canada-based Eco Atlantic announced the transfer of its 37.5 percent stake in Block 1 CBK to Israel's Navitas Petroleum, activists say they are still waiting for a clear explanation from the government about why the deal was approved.

The offshore concession, transferred in September, is located in the Orange Basin, near South Africa's maritime border with Namibia. The basin stretches along the west coasts of both countries.

According to company estimates, the block could contain more than 3.6 billion barrels of prospective oil resources, attracting growing interest from international energy companies. Some have described the Orange Basin as "Africa's Oil Frontier".

One publication described the area under Navitas's control as "one of the most active exploration regions on the African continent".

But activists monitoring the deal say Pretoria's decision to approve Navitas's entry into the project threatens South Africa's marine environment and the livelihoods of coastal communities.

They also argue that the move contradicts South Africa's position at the ICJ, where it has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza.

"Navitas is an Israeli fossil fuel company that materially benefits the Israeli economy," Tara Nair van Ryneveld of the Climate Justice Coalition told Middle East Eye.

"At a time when South Africa is pursuing international legal action concerning Israel's actions in Palestine, granting an Israeli company access to South Africa's petroleum resources raises serious questions about the consistency of our government's actions with its international obligations and stated foreign policy," van Ryneveld said.

Activists told MEE that environmental groups had raised concerns with the South African government about the proposed transaction months before Pretoria granted Navitas the necessary approvals.

'Granting an Israeli company access to South Africa's petroleum resources raises serious questions about the consistency of our government's actions'

- Tara Nair van Ryneveld, Climate Justice Coalition

In an open letter to President Cyril Ramaphosa in June, the environmental justice organisation the Green Connection called on him to explain how the transaction aligned with South Africa's international human rights commitments, particularly as the country pursued its case against Israel at the ICJ.

As a signatory to the Paris Agreement, South Africa has also committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and transitioning towards a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy.

With the deal appearing imminent, a coalition of human rights and environmental organisations, including the South African BDS Coalition, Masifundise Development Trust, Natural Justice and the Climate Justice Coalition, wrote to Mineral and Petroleum Resources Minister Gwede Mantashe and the Petroleum Agency of South Africa (Pasa) in August, urging them to reject the transfer.

On 24 September, two days after Eco Atlantic announced that the deal had been completed, the groups submitted a request to Pasa under the Promotion of Access to Information Act, seeking records relating to the approval.

Activists say neither the presidency nor Pasa has responded to their concerns in the intervening months.

"This is ultimately about South Africa's credibility as a country that upholds international human rights law," a spokesperson for The Green Connection told MEE.

Contradictory government policy

Over the past three years, South Africa has been among the few countries willing to confront Israel over its genocidal war in Gaza.

In December 2023, Pretoria brought a case against Israel at the ICJ, accusing it of violating the Genocide Convention. More than 250,000 Palestinians have been killed or injured, while more than 80 percent of structures in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed.

Towards Palestinian Liberation: How resistance travels across borders
Read More »

Despite its actions at the ICJ, South Africa has continued to sell coal to Israel, even increasing exports and becoming the country's largest coal supplier during the genocide.

Pretoria has also refused to prosecute South African citizens who joined the Israeli military, despite national legislation prohibiting citizens from serving in a foreign country's armed forces without prior authorisation.

Moreover, the presidency has declined to sever diplomatic ties with Israel, despite a parliamentary vote authorising it to do so.

Activists say the decision to allow Navitas to acquire a stake in the offshore exploration block exposes a wider gap between Pretoria's position at the ICJ and its actions at home.

"The Navitas project contradicts efforts to sanction Israel for genocide and colonial expansion. It runs counter to what the United Nations has called for, which is the isolation of Israel," a spokesperson for South African Jews for a Free Palestine (SAJFP) told MEE.

The activists say they would have opposed exploration in the block regardless of the company involved, citing risks to South Africa's marine environment.

However, they argue that approving an Israeli company's involvement deepened their objections.

'The Navitas project contradicts efforts to sanction Israel for genocide and colonial expansion'

- South African Jews for a Free Palestine spokesperson

"As offshore exploration sites pose a threat to South Africa’s coastal environments and communities, Zionism and the broader infrastructure of global extractive capitalism with which it is interdependent produces severe ecological harm everywhere," the spokesperson for SAJFP added.

Activists also argue that approving new oil and gas exploration runs counter to the urgent need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and limit global warming.

They say expanding exploration would encourage further fossil fuel production and deepen dependence on oil and gas at a time when South Africa should be moving towards cleaner energy sources.

In the Eastern Cape province, communities have waged a years-long legal battle against Shell's proposed offshore exploration along the Wild Coast.

In August, the Constitutional Court ruled against Shell and Impact Africa's oil exploration plans.

In its coverage of the legal victory against the multinational energy company, Greenpeace said the ruling "strengthens the case for African governments to move away from an economic dependence on fossil fuels and towards reliable renewable energy and green employment".

The myth of economic opportunity

Speaking at the South Africa-Namibia Bi-National Commission in July, Ramaphosa described the Orange Basin as "one of the world's most promising new energy frontiers".

The South African president said developing the basin could help build a regional energy industry spanning exploration, engineering, refining, petrochemicals, logistics, maritime services and advanced manufacturing.

Business leaders have also highlighted the prospects of investment, job creation and energy security in South Africa, where energy costs have soared.

But climate justice activists say they are sceptical of claims that ordinary South Africans would benefit from oil and gas extraction.

"This lack of transparency is deeply concerning, particularly when decisions of this scale have potentially irreversible consequences for our oceans, climate and coastal communities," van Ryneveld, from the Climate Justice Coalition, said.

Several activists pointed to academic studies suggesting that profits from offshore extraction tend to flow out of the country, leaving coastal communities to bear the environmental risks while receiving few lasting economic benefits.

'We should be investing in an energy transition that delivers lasting jobs and broader economic benefits without sacrificing our oceans or public finances'

- The Green Connection

They said communities and small-scale fishers along the country's western coast were likely to be among those most affected, while benefiting the least.

"The oil and gas economy is structured in ways that concentrate and export wealth, while leaving governments and communities to bear the costs," Power Shift Africa, a Nairobi-based think tank working on climate and development policy, said in its May 2026 report: Pipe Dreams: How oil and gas fail to deliver economic development in Africa.

The report described oil and gas extraction as an "enclave economy", in which much of the equipment and services are imported while fuel and profits are largely exported.

It added that although the oil industry could account for a substantial share of a country's gross domestic product, it did not necessarily generate significant employment.

"Meanwhile, fishing and tourism already sustain tens of thousands of livelihoods that could be threatened by seismic surveys, oil spills and other operations," The Green Connection said.

"We need to look beyond the promise of investment and ask whether this is the best use of South Africa's natural resources. The evidence suggests that offshore oil and gas risks privatising the profits.

"We should be investing in an energy transition that delivers lasting jobs and broader economic benefits without sacrificing our oceans or public finances," The Green Connection added.

MEE reached out to Navitas for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How Ceuta and migration are defining Spain's snap election
item.description:
How Ceuta and migration are defining Spain's snap election

Submitted by Olivia Hooper on Fri, 11/27/2026 - 16:08
While the vote was triggered by domestic paralysis, anti-migration sentiment has become a key campaign focus
Relatives and friends wait for the return of people who crossed into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, at Morocco’s Bab Sebta border crossing, on 2 August 2026 (Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP)
Off

Spain is heading into snap elections after a turbulent period defined by a severe housing crisis and tensions over migration, fuelled by an incident in which 70,000 migrants from Morocco entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July. 

Prime Minster Pedro Sanchez’s position became even more tenuous after Spain’s second fatal train crash of 2026, which killed 69 people in October, just a few weeks after the snap election announcement.

Ceuta has been a dominating factor on the campaign trail so far, with the migration crisis playing directly into the hands of the opposition parties. 

The consensus is that Spain’s conservative People’s Party (PP) and the far-right Vox will likely form the country’s ruling coalition, together providing enough seats to secure a 176-seat parliamentary majority. Polls suggest the PP could win about 130 seats, the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) 110, and Vox 63.

Rather than starting his campaign in Madrid, PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo soft-launched in the enclave of Ceuta shortly after the snap election was announced. The move placed migration, border security and the future of Ceuta at the core of his political messaging. 

The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla are the European Union’s only land borders with Africa. Since the Ceuta incident, an unprecedented tragedy that caused 141 deaths, Reuters estimated last month that around 10,000 migrants remained in the enclave. 

The current focus on Ceuta has overshadowed Spain’s domestic failures, namely its housing crisis. The PP and Vox recently joined forces to vote against emergency reforms aimed at protecting tenants, tabled after an 87-year-old woman, who has since died, was evicted from her home over unpaid rent. 

Border rhetoric

Across Spain, evictions reportedly affect some 25,000 people annually. During a general strike this month, an estimated four million workers took to the streets to protest soaring rent costs and the national housing deficit. 

But rather than focusing on these issues, Feijoo and Vox leader Santiago Abascal, like many right-wing western politicians, have opted to bolster their rhetoric on a hardline anti-immigration stance, presenting Ceuta as a test of the government’s ability to manage Spain’s external borders.

Feijoo has been open in blaming Rabat “for action or omission” in the migration incident. His stance starkly contrasts with the position of Sanchez, who has repeatedly said there is no evidence of any involvement by Morocco. 

Feijoo as prime minister could risk freezing bilateral relations from day one if he arrives in Rabat leading with hardline policies and ultimatums

Abascal has been highly critical of Sanchez’s leadership on Ceuta, dubbing him “the candidate of Morocco”.

If elected, Feijoo maintains his first trip would be to Morocco to establish a “red line” with King Mohammed VI, ensuring that Spain’s “territorial integrity and sovereignty” is not compromised.

Yet despite the efforts of the far right to rally anti-immigration and wider anti-Morocco sentiment as a campaign weapon, the hardline posturing is inadvertently strengthening Rabat’s hand. Calls for troop deployments or harsher border crackdowns in Ceuta ignore the fact that security relies on Rabat’s cooperation. 

This was evidenced in Ceuta. Spain deployed its army to help stabilise the border, and began to return tens of thousands of people. Such a large-scale operation, with more than 48,000 returned in 24 hours, would not have been possible without the cooperation of Moroccan security forces. 

By blaming Rabat for “action or omission”, Feijoo is effectively emphasising that Morocco has the upper hand on border security.

Bilateral relations

Amid the snap election theatrics, Morocco made its position clear at the opening of parliament on 9 October, when King Mohammed VI defended Rabat’s relationship with Spain. He also explicitly warned that Morocco would not be influenced by “pressure, threats or blackmail”.

“I wish to point out that this partnership is a sovereign choice and a voluntary commitment,” the king said.

His comments didn’t appear to sway Feijoo, who has remained steadfast in his border narrative. In an interview with El Pais published on 10 November, Feijoo was asked whether he feared reprisals from Morocco if he were to become prime minister.

Morocco's revived claim to Ceuta and Melilla is not a demand for decolonisation

In response, Feijoo referred to the Ceuta incident as an “invasion” of Spain - a term he has used on several occasions - and vowed that if elected, he would tell Morocco that Spain would never invade its land, and ask for reciprocity. 

“What I hope for is to restore confidence with Morocco and clarify who was behind this,” he said. “To know why the interior minister, the defence minister and the prime minister hid information from us.”

Feijoo added: “The two states must be allies and collaborators, because that benefits both sides. I am not an enemy of Morocco. Now, I won’t compromise on Spain’s territorial integrity.”

Three separate opinion polls published on 16 November weighed in the potential right-wing coalition’s favour, even though Sanchez’s PSOE managed to regain some popularity. 

But pairing up Feijoo and the unrelenting Abascal would mean less flexibility when it comes to diplomatic talks on all important topics with Rabat, including border security.

Considering his abrasive tone, Feijoo as prime minister could risk freezing bilateral relations from day one if he arrives in Rabat leading with hardline policies and ultimatums - a far cry from Sanchez’s soft approach.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Residents of Jordan Valley vow to remain after Israeli bulldozers raze homes
item.description:
Residents of Jordan Valley vow to remain after Israeli bulldozers raze homes

Submitted by Fayha Shalash on Sat, 11/28/2026 - 09:41
Khirbet Samra, one of Jordan Valley's last Palestinian communities, was destroyed by Israel on Sunday
Residents survey the rubble of homes, livestock shelters and water tanks demolished by Israeli forces in the Palestinian Bedouin community of Khirbet Samra in West Bank's Area C (Jess Flom / Reuters)
Off

The latest Israeli attempt to expel the Palestinian residents of Khirbet Samra, located in the northern Jordan Valley of the occupied West Bank, resulted in the demolition of all structures in the community on Sunday. 

The demolition spared nothing, not even livestock troughs, residents told Middle East Eye.

The Israeli army went further, burying the debris to ensure the residents could not salvage or reuse any of it.

Currently, the remaining residents of Khirbet Samra are living in tents provided by human rights organisations. Yet, despite everything, they say they are determined to stay.

Dhiab Daraghmeh, a resident, said that more than 15 structures were demolished, including family homes, sheep pens, shelters for young livestock, and storage areas for fodder and hay.

He said that the Israeli army arrived unexpectedly on Sunday, accompanied by bulldozers, as the residents were caught off guard, having received no prior notice.

The Israelis gave them only ten minutes to retrieve some of their belongings from their homes. This brief window allowed them to save only a few minor items.

Almost everything else was destroyed: furniture, kitchenware, gas cylinders, refrigerators, livestock troughs, as well as bathrooms, water tanks, solar panels, and fodder storage units.

'For three days, we have been living without shelter, enduring cold nights and high daytime temperatures'

- Dhiab Daraghmeh, resident

Residents now face a grim future. With winter approaching and no shelter available, families are forced to sleep in the open, while their belongings and essential supplies are left exposed to the sun and rain.

"For three days, we have been living without shelter, enduring cold nights and high daytime temperatures. We are also deeply concerned for our newborn lambs, which cannot survive in these conditions," said Daraghmeh.

The families’ needs go beyond food and humanitarian aid; primarily, they seek the right to remain on their land, to rebuild what the Israeli bulldozers destroyed and to secure protection for themselves and their livestock against the winter elements.

Settler attacks

The demolitions are part of a long-standing pattern of attacks by Israeli settlers, a campaign that has persisted for years to displace the local population, with several communities targeted across the northern Jordan Valley.

The assaults have been ongoing since 2017 and have taken various forms, including the killing of livestock and the destruction of residents' property, actions that, three months ago, forced more than half of the community’s residents to leave and relocate to the city of Tubas.

"On June 11, 2025, settlers killed about 50 of my sheep, just one of the incidents in which I have suffered significant losses. Yet, these attacks have not driven the families to leave the area," Dhiyab added.

The residents of Khirbet Samra maintain their right to remain in the community as the land is owned by the families, inherited from their ancestors.

Evictions and erasure: How Palestinian life in East Jerusalem is being extinguished
Read More »

"My grandfather lived in this area before 1977. The family resided in various locations throughout the region before Israeli harassment, along with claims that certain lands were 'nature reserves' or 'military zones', forced them to relocate to the community’s current site," he said.

Only 21 people remain in the community, after repeated attacks by settlers that, months earlier, forced more than 24 others to leave and effectively turned the small community into an open-air prison.

Another resident, Ayman Daraghmeh, said that they had asked the soldiers for permission to access drinking water, but the request was denied shortly before the bulldozers arrived to demolish the structures.

Among the items destroyed by the bulldozers was a tree that had been planted about 16 years ago.

Once a tiny sapling, it had grown over the years to become an integral part of the family’s life and their daily memories.

"I brought it here as a small sapling about 16 years ago; my children and I used to love sitting beneath it. This tree grew up alongside us, and now they have demolished everything around it," Daraghmeh said.

He said that approximately ten tons of barley were buried under the rubble, along with quantities of animal feed and the structures used to store it.

Daraghmeh estimated the material losses for the feeding troughs alone at approximately 1,500 shekels ($451) each.

“The near-daily actions of settlers have confined us to a narrow area, making us feel as though we are living in a prison, unable to move freely beyond the small patch of land where we reside,” he said.

Pattern of displacement

In its humanitarian report issued on 18 November 2026, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said that approximately 6,800 Palestinians, including more than 3,200 children, have been displaced since the beginning of 2023 due to settler attacks and associated restrictions on land access.

This displacement has affected 137 Palestinian communities, 51 of which have been completely emptied of their inhabitants.

In 2026 alone, 2,894 Palestinians were displaced as a result of settler attacks and related access restrictions. The Jordan Valley accounted for 44 percent of all displacements linked to settler attacks and access restrictions during 2026.

Mahdi Daraghmeh, head of the Al-Maleh and Bedouin Communities Council, said that for the past two years, the community has faced escalating attacks by settlers that intensified following the establishment of a nearby settler outpost.

'Settlers deliberately bring their own livestock onto these lands and keep them there, effectively preventing the residents from utilizing the area'

- Mahdi Daraghmeh, resident

He told MEE that settlers break into their homes, often calling in army and police forces, who sometimes detain the residents.

The assaults extended to seizing the natural resources upon which the residents depend for their livelihoods.

Settlers have taken control of water wells near the community, blocking families from accessing or using them. They have also seized vast areas of grazing land, preventing residents from taking their livestock out to pasture.

This pressure has further extended to rain-fed agricultural lands that families traditionally cultivated on a seasonal basis, using them for both grazing and harvesting crops.

“Settlers deliberately bring their own livestock onto these lands and keep them there, effectively preventing the residents from utilising the area,” he said.

According to Draghmeh, the Israeli army continues to maintain a daily presence in the community, threatening residents against constructing any new facilities and demanding that they leave the area.

"The residents of Khirbet Samra rely primarily on livestock farming for their livelihood. Consequently, the seizure of grazing lands and water wells along with the destruction of animal pens and fodder storage poses a direct threat to their ability to continue living in the region," he added.

According to local Palestinians, the happenings in Khirbet Samra are part of a broader pattern of attacks and encirclement targeting Bedouin communities in the northern Jordan Valley.

According to Draghmeh, six Bedouin communities have been completely depopulated, with approximately 200 families displaced in the last two years.

item.description:
Pezeshkian announces return of damaged South Pars gas pipelines to production

Iran has repaired three gas pipelines damaged in the early weeks of the US-Israeli war, returning them to production at the South Pars gas field, the country’s state-run Mehr news agency said.

The agency said that lines 1 and 4 of the fourth refinery and line 3 of the sixth refinery were back in operation, adding 20 million cubic metres of gas a day to Iran's gas output capacity.

President Masoud Pezeshkian announced the development, saying: “Getting through the winter without cutting off electricity, gas, and fuel needed for production requires the support of the people, the efforts of producers, and improving infrastructure.”

War damage to Iran’s energy infrastructure has compounded energy shortages. As winter draws close, authorities have announced two-hour electricity cuts in parts of the country.
